A conjecture is a belief or conclusion you reach through reasoning or observation — but without full, solid proof. Think of it as an educated guess: not a random stab in the dark, but not a proven fact either. It sits in the middle ground between "I'm just guessing" and "I can prove this."

When someone says "that's pure conjecture," they're pushing back on a claim, essentially saying: "You believe this, and maybe you have reasons to, but you can't actually prove it."
More Than a Guess, Less Than a Fact

This distinction is the heart of the word, so it's worth getting exactly right.

A plain guess can be completely random — like picking a number between 1 and 100. A conjecture, by contrast, is grounded in some reasoning, pattern, or observation. You have reasons to believe it. Those reasons just aren't strong enough to call it proven.

Imagine you notice your neighbour's car is missing, their lights are off, and their mailbox is overflowing. You might say: "My conjecture is that they've gone on holiday." You're not certain — maybe their car is in the shop and they've been sleeping all week — but you have logical reasons for your belief. That's a conjecture.
How It's Used in Everyday Language

In ordinary conversation, conjecture often carries a slightly skeptical or dismissive tone. It's typically used to signal that someone is reaching a conclusion they can't fully back up.

For example: "The news report about the company's collapse was based entirely on conjecture — there were no documents, no insiders, nothing concrete."

Here, calling something conjecture is a way of saying: the claim might be interesting or even plausible, but it hasn't been established as true.
How It's Used in Formal and Academic Contexts

In mathematics especially, conjecture has a precise and important role. A mathematical conjecture is a statement that mathematicians believe to be true — often because it holds up in every case they've tested — but which no one has formally proved yet.

One of the most famous examples is the Goldbach Conjecture: the claim that every even number greater than 2 can be written as the sum of two prime numbers. Mathematicians have verified this for astronomically large numbers and it always works — yet no one has proved it holds for every even number that exists. So, despite being almost certainly true, it still carries the label "conjecture."

When a conjecture is eventually proved beyond all doubt, it gets promoted to a theorem — a statement that has been conclusively established. This tells you something important about the word: even an idea that the entire mathematical world believes to be true must wear the humble label "conjecture" until the proof is airtight. The word honours intellectual honesty.
How It Compares to Similar Words

Speculation is the closest word to conjecture and the two are often used interchangeably. If anything, speculation can be even looser — you can speculate with very little reasoning at all. Conjecture implies slightly more deliberate thought behind the belief.

Hypothesis (particularly in science) is more structured. A hypothesis is a specific, testable prediction: "If I do X, then Y will happen." A conjecture is a more general belief or claim that hasn't been formally tested or proved.

Assumption is something you accept as true without really examining it closely. You often make assumptions automatically, without consciously working through any reasoning. A conjecture is more deliberate — you've thought about it, you have reasons, you just can't prove it.

Theory, in the scientific sense, is far stronger than a conjecture. A scientific theory is supported by a large, well-tested body of evidence accumulated over time. A conjecture is still waiting for that kind of support.
The Tone and Register of the Word

"Conjecture" is a moderately formal word. In casual conversation, people tend to reach for "guess," "hunch," or "theory" instead. You'll encounter "conjecture" more often in writing, academic discourse, journalism, courtrooms, and mathematics. Using it in everyday speech gives your language a slightly precise, intellectual flavour.

A conjecture is a reasoned belief or conclusion that hasn't yet been proved. It's more than a random guess — there's logic or evidence pointing toward it — but it's less than a fact, because the proof is missing or incomplete. It lives in that honest, uncertain space where intelligent thinking happens before certainty arrives. And the moment it is proved, it stops being a conjecture entirely.
